::: {#def-operator-precedence}

## Operator precedence

**Operator precedence** is the convention that decides
which operator in an unparenthesized expression applies first,
as when $2 + 3 \cdot 4$ means $2 + (3 \cdot 4)$.

:::

Write parentheses that make [operator precedence](#def-operator-precedence) explicit,
rather than leaving the reader to recall the convention.
A reader who is still learning the notation
may not know
whether $\lor$ binds more tightly than $\in$,
and a reader who knows the convention still has to stop and apply it.
Parentheses answer the question on the page.

Two cases come up most often:

- **A relation beside a connective.**
  Parenthesize each comparison or membership
  that is an operand of a [logical connective](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mcs/chapters/propositional-logic.html#def-logical-connective)
  such as $\land$, $\lor$, $\Rightarrow$, or $\Leftrightarrow$.
- **Two kinds of connective together.**
  Parenthesize whenever two different connectives share one level.
  Also parenthesize a repeated [implication](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mcs/chapters/propositional-logic.html#def-implies)
  or a repeated [biconditional](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mcs/chapters/propositional-logic.html#def-iff),
  because readers do not share a convention for how a chain of them groups,
  and the two groupings of a chained implication are different propositions.
  A repeated $\land$ or a repeated $\lor$ needs no parentheses,
  because every grouping of it has the same meaning.

::: {#exm-precedence-parentheses-relations}

## Parenthesizing relations beside a connective

> ❌ $\set{x : x \in A \lor x \in B}$ <!-- check-precedence-parens: allow -->
>
> ✅ $\set{x : (x \in A) \lor (x \in B)}$

> ❌ $x > 0 \Rightarrow x^2 > 0$ <!-- check-precedence-parens: allow -->
>
> ✅ $(x > 0) \Rightarrow (x^2 > 0)$

:::

::: {#exm-precedence-parentheses-connectives}

## Parenthesizing two kinds of connective

> ❌ $P \land Q \lor R$ <!-- check-precedence-parens: allow -->
>
> ✅ $(P \land Q) \lor R$

:::

A separator already ends an operand,
so it needs no parentheses of its own.
The separators are the colon of a [set builder](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mcs/chapters/sets.html#def-set-builder),
the comma that ends a [quantifier](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mcs/chapters/predicates-quantifiers.html#def-quantifier), as in $\forall x \in A, P(x)$,
and a definition sign.

The `check-precedence-parens` check,
which [gha#2118](https://github.com/Morrison-Lab/gha/pull/2118) adds to gha,
fails a pull request that adds math breaking either rule.
Mark a line that shows an ungrouped form on purpose,
such as an exercise that asks which grouping is meant,
with `<!-- check-precedence-parens: allow -->`.
